doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Meyer mouthpiece and groove records
summary: Earl Bostic's mouthpiece advice gave him a clearer sound and he focused on groove records.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I want to ask about the way you developed your group sound in the ‘60s. Alligator Boogaloo or Midnight Creeper are a very different sound and approach than, well, Lush Life, but also the records with Big John Patton four-five years before.

Can you speak about evolving towards that way of thinking about making records and your sound, and how it reflected the audiences you were playing for and what was going on around in the music, which was changing in the ‘60s...

I met Earl Bostic in ‘57, and he told me... I was playing a Brilhart mouthpiece, and he told me, “Get rid of that and get a Meyer.” He said a Meyer is better for the Selmer saxophone. He was right, and I got a different sound. Much clearer. I got the new sound, so I started playing slightly different. Not much. Slightly different.

Well, I started making a lot of groove records. The groove records depend on the groove. You don’t have to worry about anything else really but the groove. Because if you’ve got the right tempo, and everything is hitting where it’s supposed to hit, you’re in business. You can play variations on it, do anything on it, but if the groove is there, you’re in business.
Are you saying you started to do that in ‘57-‘58, after you got...
Those earlier records seem to be a mixture of those sorts of tunes, and bebop tunes and popular tunes and blueses...
Yeah. It was a mixture of bebop and swing. That was the formula we used. And all those records were selling, too.
